pronunciation-long-and-short-vowels/pron:
English has pairs of vowels that many learners hear as one sound. The most important is /iː/ as in sheep, see, green, and /ɪ/ as in ship, sit, fish.

The /iː/ sound is **long and tense**: spread your lips slightly, as if you are about to smile, and keep your tongue high and forward. The /ɪ/ sound is **short and relaxed**: the tongue is a little lower and further back, and the lips are loose.

Length helps, but the shape of the mouth matters more; a long /ɪ/ still sounds like ship. Common spellings for /iː/ are ee, ea, e-e and ie (see, eat, these, piece); /ɪ/ is usually a single i or y (sit, gym).

The back vowels work the same way. /uː/ as in food, blue, moon is **long and tense**, with rounded lips pushed slightly forward, as if you are about to whistle. /ʊ/ as in book, good, foot is **short and relaxed**, with only lightly rounded lips.

Spelling does not help much here:
- oo can be either sound (food /uː/, good /ʊ/)
- u can be either (rule /uː/, put /ʊ/).

Learn common words in pairs and say them aloud together:
- pool – pull
- fool – full
- Luke – look.

A **minimal pair** is two words that differ in only one sound, like sheep and ship. Minimal pairs train your ear and your mouth together:
- First listen to both words and notice the difference.
- Then say each word slowly, exaggerating the mouth shape, and gradually speed up to normal.
- Finally, put the words in short sentences, because sounds change a little in real speech.

If the phone hears the other word of the pair, it is a useful signal: go back to the mouth position, not just the length.
pronunciation-open-vowels/pronunciation-:
The vowel /e/ as in bed, red, ten is made with the mouth **half open** and the tongue in the middle-front of the mouth. The vowel /æ/ as in cat, bad, map needs a **wider mouth**: drop your jaw and spread your lips, and let the tongue lie low at the front.

Many learners say both as /e/, so bad sounds like bed and man like men. A good test is to put a finger on your chin: it should move down further for /æ/.

In American English /æ/ is often a little longer than in British English.

The vowel /ʌ/ as in cup, bus, sun is **short and central**: the mouth is relaxed and slightly open, and the tongue sits in the middle. The vowel /ɑː/ as in father, calm, palm is **long and open at the back**, with the jaw down and the tongue low.

In American English, words like hot, cop and lock also use an open /ɑ/ sound, while British English uses a short rounded /ɒ/.

The key contrast for most learners is between the short, central /ʌ/ (cup, luck) and the open back vowel (cop, lock).

Front and open vowels form a **ladder**: /iː/ (see) at the top, then /ɪ/ (sit), /e/ (bed), and /æ/ (bad) at the bottom. Slide slowly down the ladder — see, sit, set, sat — and feel your jaw open a little more at each step. This makes the differences physical rather than only something you try to hear.

Use a mirror or your phone’s camera: if your mouth does not change between bed and bad, the listener will not hear a difference either.
pronunciation-schwa-and-weak-syllables/p:
The **schwa /ə/** is the most common vowel sound in English. It is short, quiet and relaxed — like the sound you make when you hesitate: "uh". It appears in **unstressed syllables**, whatever the spelling:
- the a in about
- the o in today
- the e in problem
- the u in support
- the er in teacher (in British English).

Native speakers rarely pronounce every vowel fully. Saying banana as ba-NA-na with three clear a sounds sounds foreign; natural English is /bəˈnɑːnə/, with two schwas.

Learning to relax the unstressed syllables is one of the fastest ways to sound more natural.

Many short grammar words — a, the, to, of, for, and, can, was, have — have a **strong form** and a **weak form**. In normal speech they are unstressed, so they use the weak form with a schwa:
- to becomes /tə/
- of becomes /əv/ or even /ə/
- and becomes /ən/ or /n/
- can becomes /kən/.

"A cup of tea" sounds like "a cuppa tea"; "fish and chips" sounds like "fish ’n’ chips".

Use the strong form only when the word is stressed for meaning, or at the end of a phrase: "Yes, I CAN." "Where are you from?"

Because so many syllables are weak, English rhythm is made of **strong beats** separated by quick, weak syllables. This is why fast English can be hard to understand: the weak syllables almost disappear.

When you listen, focus on the stressed words; the weak ones fill themselves in from context.

When you speak, do the opposite of what feels natural to many learners: say the stressed syllables clearly and let the weak ones be short and relaxed.
pronunciation-diphthongs/pronunciation-d:
A **diphthong** is a vowel that **glides** from one position to another within one syllable. Your tongue and lips move during the sound. English has several:
- /eɪ/ as in day
- /aɪ/ as in time
- /ɔɪ/ as in boy
- /aʊ/ as in now
- /əʊ/ (British) or /oʊ/ (American) as in go.

Learners often make these too short or keep the mouth still, so late sounds like let, and time sounds like tame. Make the glide clear: start at the first position and move smoothly to the second.

Two diphthongs end with the lips rounding. **/aʊ/** as in now, house, town starts wide open, like /æ/ or /a/, and closes towards a rounded /ʊ/. **/əʊ/** (British) or /oʊ/ (American) as in go, home, road starts in the middle and rounds towards /ʊ/.

If you keep the lips still, now can sound like no, and town like tone; if you do not round at all, boat can sound like bought. Watch your lips in a mirror: they should move during the vowel.

Diphthongs have **many spellings**. /eɪ/: a-e (late), ai (rain), ay (day), ei (eight).
- /aɪ/: i-e (time), y (my), igh (light).
- /ɔɪ/: oi (coin), oy (boy).
- /aʊ/: ou (house), ow (now).
- /əʊ/: o-e (home), oa (boat), ow (show).

Notice that ow has two sounds: now /aʊ/ and show /əʊ/. When you learn a new word, check its sound in a dictionary and say it aloud, rather than guessing from the letters.
pronunciation-r-coloured-vowels/pronunci:
The vowel /ɜː/ as in bird, turn, learn, word is **long and central**. Keep your lips neutral (not rounded, not spread) and your tongue in the middle of the mouth.

In American English the tongue also curls or bunches for an r sound, so bird is /bɝd/.

Many learners replace it with /e/, /ʌ/ or /ɔː/: bird becomes bud, and work becomes walk. Its spellings are varied:
- ir (bird)
- ur (turn)
- er (her)
- ear (learn)
- after w (word, work, world).

The vowel in car, park, heart is **long and open at the back**: /ɑː/ in British English, /ɑr/ in American English.

The vowel in door, short, north is **long and rounded**: /ɔː/ in British English, /ɔr/ in American English.

Keep these long. If you make them short, heart can sound like hot, and short like shot. Round your lips for /ɔː/ and keep them open and relaxed for /ɑː/.

English accents differ in how they treat the letter r after a vowel. In **rhotic accents** — most American, Canadian, Scottish and Irish English — you pronounce it: car /kɑr/. In **non-rhotic accents** — most of England, Australia and New Zealand — the r is silent unless a vowel follows: car /kɑː/, but "car engine" links with an r.

Both are correct. Choose one model and be consistent; mixing them in one sentence sounds odd. Either way, the vowel before the r should be long.
pronunciation-voiced-and-voiceless-pairs:
Many English consonants come in pairs made in the same place in the mouth. The only difference is **voicing**: whether your vocal cords vibrate.

Put your fingers on your throat and say a long "sssss" then "zzzzz". You will feel a buzz for /z/ but not for /s/. The pairs are:
- /p/–/b/
- /t/–/d/
- /k/–/ɡ/
- /f/–/v/
- /s/–/z/
- /θ/–/ð/
- /ʃ/–/ʒ/
- /tʃ/–/dʒ/.

The first of each pair is voiceless, the second voiced. Getting this wrong changes meaning:
- pig and big
- fan and van
- sip and zip.

At the start of a stressed syllable, English /p/, /t/ and /k/ are **aspirated**: they are followed by a small puff of air.

Hold a piece of paper in front of your mouth and say pen: the paper should move. Say Ben and it should not.

In many languages /p/, /t/, /k/ have no puff, so English listeners hear them as /b/, /d/, /ɡ/: pear can sound like bear, and coat like goat. Add a clear puff to /p/, /t/, /k/ at the beginning of words.

At the end of a word, voicing also changes the vowel before it: the vowel is **longer before a voiced consonant**. Compare bet (short vowel, /t/) with bed (longer vowel, /d/), and back with bag.

Many learners drop the final consonant or devoice it, so bed sounds like bet. Lengthen the vowel slightly before voiced endings and finish the consonant clearly.

This is especially important for past tense -ed and plural -s, which carry grammar.
pronunciation-th-sounds/pronunciation-th:
English has two TH sounds, and few other languages have them. Both are made the same way: put the tip of your tongue lightly between your top and bottom teeth, or just behind your top teeth, and blow air gently over it. The **voiceless /θ/** in think, three, bath has no buzz. The **voiced /ð/** in this, that, mother has a buzz.

Learners often replace them with /s/, /t/, /f/ (think → sink, tink or fink) or /z/, /d/ (this → zis, dis). Show your tongue tip — a mirror helps.

The **voiced /ð/** is very common in small grammar words: the, this, that, these, those, they, them, there, than, then, though. It also appears between vowels in words like mother, father, weather, together. The **voiceless /θ/** appears in most content words: think, thank, thing, three, Thursday, health, month, birthday.

Some pairs differ only in TH:
- teeth (noun, /θ/) and teethe (verb, /ð/)
- bath (noun) and bathe (verb).

In **connected speech**, TH words can blend with neighbouring sounds. In "in the", the /n/ and /ð/ often merge; in "what’s that", the /s/ and /ð/ are close together.

Don’t slow down so much that every TH becomes heavy, but keep the tongue forward so the sound is still TH. Practise phrases rather than single words:
- "thank you"
- "think about it"
- "one of the three"
- "this and that".

A light, quick TH is more natural than an exaggerated one.
pronunciation-s-sh-ch-and-j/pronunciatio:
For **/s/** as in see, sun, rice, the tongue tip is close to the ridge behind your top teeth, the lips are spread, and air hisses through a narrow gap. For **/ʃ/** as in she, shoe, wish, the tongue pulls back a little, the lips round and push forward, and the sound is softer and deeper — like asking someone to be quiet: "shhh". Confusing them changes meaning:
- see / she
- sip / ship
- sea / she
- mess / mesh.

The voiced partner of /ʃ/ is /ʒ/, as in measure, vision, usually.

The sound **/tʃ/** as in chip, chair, watch is a /t/ followed immediately by /ʃ/. Start with your tongue blocking the air, then release it into the "shh" sound.

If there is no stop at the start, chip sounds like ship and choose like shoes. The voiced partner is **/dʒ/** as in jam, job, bridge. Spellings:
- ch and tch for /tʃ/ (chair, watch)
- j, g and dge for /dʒ/ (job, gym, bridge).

The letter y at the start of a word is a **glide /j/**, as in yes, yellow, young: the tongue rises towards the roof of the mouth but does not touch it.

The /dʒ/ in jet, joke, jam has a full stop: the tongue touches the roof of the mouth, then releases.

Speakers of some languages swap them, so yet sounds like jet, or jam like yam. The /j/ sound also hides inside some words:
- use /juːz/
- music /ˈmjuːzɪk/
- few /fjuː/.
pronunciation-l-r-w-v-h-and-ng/pronuncia:
For /l/ as in light, long, feel, the tongue tip **touches the ridge** behind the top teeth and air flows around the sides of the tongue.

For the English /r/ as in right, red, road, the tongue tip **does not touch anything**: it curls back slightly or bunches up, and the lips round a little.

Many learners swap them, so light sounds like right, or lead like read. Practise the tongue touch:
- for /l/ you should feel contact
- for /r/ there should be no contact at all.

For /w/ as in we, wet, west, **round your lips tightly**, as if to blow out a candle, and then open them into the vowel. Your teeth do not touch your lip.

For /v/ as in van, very, vest, put your **top teeth gently on your lower lip** and let the voice buzz through.

If you use your teeth for /w/, wet sounds like vet; if you only round your lips for /v/, vest sounds like west. Check in a mirror:
- teeth on lip for /v/
- rounded lips only for /w/.

The sound **/h/** as in hat, home, behind is simply a breath of air before a vowel, with the mouth already in the shape of that vowel. Some learners drop it (hat → at), and others add a rough, scraping sound from the throat; English /h/ is gentle. The sound **/ŋ/** as in sing, long, thing is made with the back of the tongue against the soft palate, like /ɡ/ but with air through the nose.

At the end of a word, do not add a /ɡ/ after it in standard British or American English: sing is /sɪŋ/, not /sɪŋɡ/. And keep it different from /n/: sin and sing are different words.
pronunciation-word-stress/pronunciation-:
In English words of two or more syllables, **one syllable is stressed**: it is louder, longer and higher in pitch, with a full vowel. The others are weaker, often with a schwa.

PHOtograph, phoTOgraphy, photoGRAPHic — the stress moves, and the vowels change with it. Stress is part of how a word is recognised. If you stress the wrong syllable, listeners may not understand the word even when every sound is correct.

Dictionaries mark stress with a small vertical line before the stressed syllable: /ˈfəʊtəɡrɑːf/.

There are no perfect rules, but some patterns help:
- Most two-syllable nouns and adjectives are stressed on the **first syllable**: TAble, HAPpy, WINdow.
- Most two-syllable verbs are stressed on the **second**: deCIDE, beGIN, reLAX.
- Some words change stress with their job: a PREsent (noun), to preSENT (verb); a REcord, to reCORD.
- **Suffixes** often decide the stress: words ending in -tion, -sion and -ic are stressed on the syllable just before the ending (eduCAtion, deCIsion, ecoNOMic).
- **Compound nouns** are usually stressed on the first part: BUS stop, BEDroom, TOOTHbrush.

Clap, tap or nod on the **stressed syllable** as you say a word: ba-NA-na. Make that syllable clearly louder and longer, and let the others shrink.

When you learn a new word, learn its stress at the same time; mark it in your notes with capitals or a dot above the syllable.

Pay attention to **word families**, where the stress moves: eCOnomy, ecoNOMic, eCOnomist; PHOtograph, phoTOgrapher. Say them in a row to feel the shift.
pronunciation-sentence-stress-and-rhythm:
In a sentence, not every word is stressed. **Content words** — nouns, main verbs, adjectives, adverbs and negatives — carry the meaning and are usually stressed. **Function words** — articles, pronouns, prepositions, auxiliaries and conjunctions — are usually unstressed and use weak forms.

"I WANT to GO HOME." "She’s BEEN to PAris TWICE."

If you stress every word equally, your English sounds mechanical and is harder to follow. If you stress the content words, listeners can pick out the message even when they miss the small words.

English rhythm is based on **stressed syllables**. The time between stressed syllables stays roughly the same, so the unstressed syllables between them are squeezed to fit.

Say "CATS EAT FISH" and then "The CATS will have EATen the FISH": the second sentence takes only a little longer, because the extra words are squeezed.

Many languages give every syllable equal time, which can make English sound choppy when transferred. Let the weak syllables run together and land on the beats.

In connected speech, words **link together**. A consonant at the end of a word links to a vowel at the start of the next:
- "an apple" sounds like "a-napple"
- "turn off" like "tur-noff".

Some sounds disappear between consonants: "next day" often sounds like "nex day".

Stress can also move to show **contrast** or correction: "I said the BLUE one" (not the red one), "SHE called" (not he). Moving the stress is a powerful way to clarify what you mean without extra words.
pronunciation-intonation/pronunciation-i: **Intonation** is the rise and fall of your voice across a sentence. It adds meaning beyond the words. A **falling tune** at the end usually signals that you are finished and certain: statements, commands, and questions that start with a question word. "I live in Paris." "Close the door." "Where do you live?" A **rising tune** often signals a yes/no question, surprise, or that you have not finished: "Are you ready?" "Really?" The movement happens mainly on the last stressed word of the phrase.

In a **list**, the voice usually rises on each item and falls on the last, so the listener knows the list is complete: "I bought apples ↗, bread ↗ and milk ↘." In a **choice question**, the voice rises on the first option and falls on the last: "Do you want tea ↗ or coffee ↘?" **Question tags** change meaning with intonation:
- A falling tag expects agreement: "It’s cold, isn’t it ↘?"
- A rising tag is a real question: "You’re coming, aren’t you ↗?"

Using these patterns makes your meaning clear without extra words.

Intonation also shows **attitude**. A wide range — big rises and falls — sounds interested, warm or excited; a narrow, flat range can sound bored, tired or even rude, whatever the words.

"Thank you" said with a clear fall sounds sincere; said flat and quick it can sound dismissive.

English speakers use more pitch movement than speakers of many other languages, so learners often need to exaggerate slightly to sound natural. Listen to how native speakers say short reactions — "Really?", "Oh no!", "That’s great!" — and copy the tune, not only the words.
reading-listening-topic-gist-and-support:
The **gist** is the big idea of a text: what it is mostly about. Before looking for small facts, read the whole text once, quickly, and ask, "What is this about?"

Look at the title, any pictures, and the first and last sentences; they often carry the main idea.

Do not stop for every new word. Most unknown words do not change the gist, and stopping breaks your understanding of the whole.

When you have finished, try to say the gist in one short sentence. If you can, you are ready to look for details.

A **detail** is a single fact: a name, a place, a time, a number, a reason.

To find details efficiently, read the question first, so you know what you are looking for. The question word tells you what kind of detail to find:
- who → a person
- when → a time
- where → a place
- how many → a number
- why → a reason (often after because).

Then go back to the text and look for words that match or mean the same as the question. Check the sentences around your answer to make sure it fits exactly.
reading-listening-topic-scanning-and-lis:
**Scanning** means moving your eyes quickly over a text to find one specific piece of information, without reading every word. It is how you use a timetable, a menu, a phone list or a search result.

Before you scan, decide exactly what you are looking for and what it will look like:
- a capital letter for a name
- digits for a number or price
- a day or month name for a date.

Let your eyes move down the page looking for that shape, then stop and read carefully around it.

When you listen, you usually cannot go back, so you cannot catch every word. Focus on the **key words**: names, numbers, places, times and main verbs.

In English, these content words are stressed — said louder and longer — while small words like the, a, to and of are quick and quiet.

Before listening, predict what you might hear from the situation: at a train station, expect platforms, times and destinations. While listening, ask yourself: who is speaking, what do they want, and when or where?
reading-listening-topic-main-ideas-and-c:
The **main idea** is the single most important point of a text or paragraph; the other sentences support it with details, examples and reasons.

Writers often state it in the first sentence, sometimes in the last. To check, ask: which idea are most of the sentences about?

Be careful not to choose an idea that is too narrow (a single detail) or too broad (bigger than the text). A good main-idea sentence could be the title of the paragraph.

When you meet a new word, keep reading — the words around it often explain it. Look for **clues**: a synonym or definition ("enormous, or very large"), an opposite ("Unlike his outgoing sister, Tom is shy"), an example ("citrus fruits, such as lemons and oranges"), or the general situation. Also notice the type of word: is it a noun, a verb, an adjective? Then guess the meaning and check that the sentence still makes sense. Use a dictionary afterwards for words you meet often or that seem essential.
reading-listening-topic-signals-facts-an:
**Signal words** are small words and phrases that show how ideas connect and what is coming next:
- Addition: and, also, in addition.
- Contrast: but, however, although.
- Reason: because, since.
- Result: so, therefore, as a result.
- Example: for example, such as.
- Sequence: first, then, finally.
- Conclusion: in conclusion, overall.

Noticing them helps you predict the next idea and follow the writer’s or speaker’s thinking. A however often signals that the most important point is about to come.

A **fact** can be checked and shown to be true or false: "The bridge is 300 metres long." An **opinion** expresses what someone thinks, feels or believes, and people can reasonably disagree: "The bridge is beautiful."

Signals of opinion include I think, I believe, in my view, should, must, and judging words such as best, worst, beautiful, terrible, important.

Many texts mix the two. Separating them helps you decide what to accept as information and what to treat as someone’s view.
reading-listening-topic-skimming-and-par:
Skimming and scanning are both fast reading skills, used for different purposes.

**Skimming** means reading quickly to get the general idea: look at the title, headings, the first sentence of each paragraph and the last paragraph.

**Scanning** means searching for one specific fact — a name, a number, a date — without reading everything.

Use them together: skim first to understand what the text is and where things are, then scan the right section for the detail you need. Neither involves stopping at every unknown word.

A well-written paragraph usually develops one main idea. The **topic sentence** states that idea, most often at the start.

The other sentences support it with details, examples, reasons or explanations, and a final sentence may conclude or lead to the next paragraph.

Reading the first sentence of each paragraph lets you follow a long text quickly. To check your understanding, try to label each paragraph in a few words: "causes", "an example", "the solution".
reading-listening-topic-reference-and-se:
Writers avoid repeating nouns by using **reference words**: pronouns (it, they, them, he, she), demonstratives (this, that, these, those) and phrases such as the former, the latter, such.

To understand a text, you need to know what each one points to.

Usually it refers to the nearest earlier noun that fits in number and meaning. This and that can refer to a whole idea, not just a noun. If you are unsure, replace the reference word with the noun or idea and check that the sentence still makes sense.

Instructions, processes and stories often use **sequence words** to show order: first, then, next, after that, before, while, finally. They help you picture what happens and in which order.

When following instructions, number the steps as you read.

Be careful with before and after: in "Before you serve it, add salt", adding salt comes first even though it is mentioned second. Time expressions — at first, later, the next day, eventually — do the same job in stories.
reading-listening-topic-numbers-and-spok:
Numbers go by fast in speech, and some sound alike. Listen for the **stress**: thirTEEN, fourTEEN, fifTEEN have stress at the end; THIRty, FORty, FIFty at the start.

Times can be said in different ways: "half past four", "four thirty", "sixteen thirty". Prices are often said without the currency word for the cents: "twelve fifty" usually means 12.50.

Write numbers as digits while you listen, and check any important number by repeating it back.

To follow spoken instructions, listen for three things: **action verbs** (turn, press, open, wait, take), **order words** (first, then, after) and numbers or places.

Make very short notes as you listen: "L, 2nd st, R at bank".

If you miss a step, ask politely: "Sorry, could you repeat the last part?" At the end, repeat the whole set back to check: "So I turn left, walk two streets, then turn right at the bank?" This catches mistakes before you act on them.
reading-listening-topic-speakers-purpose:
Before and during listening, ask: Who is speaking? Who are they speaking to? What do they want? The answers help you predict words and understand meaning.

A shop assistant, a friend and a news reader all speak differently. Listen for clues in the greeting, the vocabulary and the tone — friendly, formal, worried, annoyed.

The **purpose** may be to inform, ask, invite, complain, apologise, persuade or thank. Understanding the purpose often helps you guess the parts you did not catch.

You cannot write every word while listening, so note only the **key words**: names, numbers, places, dates and actions. Use short forms and symbols: Mon, 3pm, →, @, +, ↑ (increase), ✗ (no).

Leave out small words such as a, the and is. After listening, use your notes to write one or two full sentences while your memory is fresh.

If you miss something, leave a gap and keep listening; trying to catch up on one word can make you miss the next three.
reading-listening-topic-inference-purpos:
Writers do not always say everything directly. An **inference** is a conclusion you reach from clues in the text combined with what you already know.

If a story says that a man shook rain from his umbrella and stamped his wet boots, you can infer that it is raining, even though the text never says so.

Good inferences fit all the clues and do not go beyond them. Ask: what clues support this? Is there another possible explanation?

Every text has a **purpose**: to inform, persuade, entertain, instruct or warn.

**Tone** is the writer’s attitude towards the subject and the reader: neutral, enthusiastic, critical, humorous, worried. Word choice is the main clue:
- "A tragic mistake" is critical
- "a few changes" is neutral
- "an incredible opportunity" is enthusiastic.

Asking "Why was this written, and by whom?" helps you decide how far to trust it: an advertisement wants you to buy; a report wants you to understand.
reading-listening-topic-arguments-and-su:
An argument has a **claim** (what the writer wants you to accept), reasons and evidence, and often a **counterclaim** (the other side) with a response.

Find the claim first; it is often in the introduction or conclusion. Then find the reasons: words like because, since and therefore signal them.

Words like but, however, although and some people argue signal an opposing view. A strong text deals fairly with the other side.

Finally, judge: do the reasons and evidence actually support the claim?

A **summary** gives the main points of a text in your own words, much shorter than the original.

Find the main idea and the two or three most important supporting points. Leave out examples, repetition and minor details, and do not add your own opinion.

Use reporting phrases to show these are someone else’s ideas: "The writer argues that…", "According to the report…". A good summary makes sense to someone who has not read the original.
reading-listening-topic-attitude-and-lec:
In speech, how something is said can change its meaning. **Stress** shows what the speaker thinks is important or contrasting: "I didn’t say HE took it" (someone else did) is different from "I didn’t SAY he took it" (I suggested it).

**Intonation** matters too: a falling tone usually signals certainty or a statement; a rising tone often signals a question, doubt or an unfinished thought.

**Tone of voice** can even reverse the words: "Oh, great" said in a flat voice often means the opposite. Listen to the music of speech as well as the words.

In talks and lectures, speakers signal structure:
- "There are three reasons…"
- "Let me give an example…"
- "The key point is…"
- "To sum up…".

Listen for these **signposts** and use them to organise your notes. Try a simple layout:
- main points on the left, details and examples on the right
- short numbered lists.

Mark questions you want to ask with a "?". Review your notes the same day, fill in gaps and add a one-line summary at the top while you still remember.
reading-listening-topic-comparing-source:
When two texts describe the same event, compare them carefully:
- Which facts do both include?
- Which appear in only one?
- Do the numbers match?
- Is one more detailed, more recent or more careful in its language?
- Do they use different words for the same thing?

Differences can come from different sources, different times or different attitudes.

Start by listing the facts **both agree on**, then examine the differences and look for a reason for each.

**Bias** is a leaning towards one side.

**Loaded words** carry strong feelings: "The council forced through a pointless lane" is more loaded than "The council approved a new lane". Other signs of bias include:
- one-sided evidence
- missing voices (only one side is quoted)
- phrases like obviously or everyone knows.

A biased text is not necessarily false, but you should check its claims in another source. A useful exercise: replace loaded words with neutral ones and see what facts remain.
reading-listening-topic-implication-and-:
Writers often mean more, less or the opposite of what they literally say:
- **Irony** says one thing while signalling another: praising a train company’s "reliable" timetable and then advising readers to allow an extra hour.
- **Understatement** deliberately plays something down: "a slight delay" for a day of chaos.
- **Implication** leaves a conclusion unsaid for the reader to draw.

To read these, notice the gap between the words and the situation, and ask what the writer wants you to conclude.

Persuasive texts use recognisable moves:
- A **false dilemma** offers only two options.
- A **loaded contrast** sets "us" against "them" or good against bad.
- **Rhetorical questions** imply an answer.
- Repetition builds emotion.
- Appeals to authority or fear can stand in for evidence.

Spotting a move does not mean the argument is wrong; it means you should look past the style to the evidence. Ask: what am I being asked to believe or do, and what support is given?
reading-listening-topic-evidence-and-syn:
When a text cites research, ask how the study was done:
- Who took part, how many, and how were they chosen?
- Was there a comparison (control) group?
- Who paid for it, and could that influence the result?
- Does the conclusion go further than the data allows?

A claim that one thing causes another needs more than a **correlation**. Treat a single study with caution and look for others that repeat the result.

The question is not whether a study is perfect, but how far its conclusion can be trusted.

**Synthesis** means building one view from several sources, rather than summarising each in turn.

Group the sources by idea: where do they agree, where do they disagree, and do they answer different questions? Weigh their quality: sample, method, date.

Then state a position that accounts for all of them, and attribute each point: "Surveys of managers suggest gains, but a controlled trial with call-centre staff found losses, so the effect may depend on the type of work."
reading-listening-topic-long-talks-and-r:
In a long lecture or talk, speakers digress, go back, qualify and repeat. Follow the main thread by listening for **signposts**: "To return to my main point…", "The second issue is…", "In other words…".

Separate main points from asides: "By the way…", "That reminds me…" often mark a digression.

Keep a running outline, leave gaps for what you miss, and use the speaker’s summary at the end to check and complete it. If you lose the thread, do not panic — rejoin at the next signpost.

Natural speech is not careful dictionary speech. Words **blend and reduce**: going to becomes "gonna", want to becomes "wanna", did you sounds like "didja", and of often becomes a short "uh".

Small function words are weak and fast, while content words carry the stress. Accents vary in vowels, consonants and rhythm, so familiar words can sound new.

To train your ear, listen to the same short clip several times, check with captions afterwards, and focus first on the stressed words. Context often fills the gaps.
reading-listening-topic-debates-and-shif:
In debates and interviews, speakers disagree, interrupt and talk over each other. Keep track of who holds which position: note each speaker’s claim in a word or two. Listen for **stance markers** that show attitude: frankly, I’d argue that, to be fair, with respect.

Notice when a speaker **concedes** ("I accept that…"), **deflects** (answers a different question) or changes the subject. Do not confuse a speaker repeating an opponent’s view ("You say that…") with their own. Afterwards, summarise each position in one sentence.

Skilled speakers and writers often **change tone** within one piece: from formal to personal, serious to playful, distant to direct.

Notice the signals: shorter sentences, everyday vocabulary, contractions, humour, or direct address to "you". A shift often marks something important — moving from policy language to a personal story can signal the emotional centre of a speech.

Ask what the shift does for the audience. Reading tone means hearing how the speaker stands towards the topic and the listener.
